<reason>A high-quality debate. B had the more original case ("legal is not built," the crash sitting mid-window, land-option uplift, sprawl-vs-density) and landed real hits: the clipped Rebuttal 1 still forced A's "empty in 2009" concession, exposed A's abandonment of its own price-to-income yardstick, and showed A's cheapest exhibits (Houston, Phoenix) are sprawl stories rather than density stories. But A won the decisive clash. B's affirmative mechanism requires housing in high-demand cities to be nearly price-inelastic to supply — "demand swamps every unit" — which A correctly framed as claiming housing is the only good whose price ignores its quantity. B's record-based evidence (Seattle, Denver got pricier while building) never isolates the counterfactual; A repeatedly demanded the honest comparison (Seattle with cranes vs. Seattle with cranes banned) and B's closing answer ("Seattle IS the cranes case") conflates a demand-growth observation with a supply-effect test. A also answered the crash point more completely than B answered the counterfactual challenge: units built 2004–07 persist, multifamily rebounded by 2011, and "busts are cyclical, bans are permanent" captures why five bad years don't erase a twenty-year stock. Under the motion's modest "more affordable" standard, B had to show net effect ≤ 0 and mostly argued magnitude offsets; A only needed direction and defended it with vacancy, filtering, and stock-compounding mechanisms plus Austin's falling rents and Minneapolis's unanswered post-reform stability. B's option-value answer to A's pressure question was honest and coherent, and the yardstick hit was real, which keeps this competitive — but A's path to the motion as written was cleaner and less neutralized.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>A's Rebuttal 1 reversal — "when CON says filtering takes decades, note what this motion hands us: two decades" — plus the Manhattan counterfactual ("towers vs. a Manhattan where towers were banned") set the comparative frame B never squarely engaged; B's best counter was the Rebuttal 2 attack on A's abandoned price-to-income yardstick, damaging but not decisive.</best_rebuttal>
